The bank under Lionel financed the British government's £4M purchase of Egypt's Suez Canal shares (1875).

Nov 1917: co-founder and first president of the League of British Jews.
Sir Philip Magnus, vice-president.
Louis Montagu, 2nd Baron Swaythling, vice-president.
Anti-Zionist: opposed the declaration and the claim that Jews are a separate nationality.
18 July 1917: Walter sent Balfour the 46-word draft formula.
1902-03: Colonial Secretary Chamberlain, who knew Herzl through the Rothschilds, discussed Cyprus, Sinai and El Arish, then proposed East Africa.
The British offer of East African land for Jewish settlement (1903).
Chamberlain agreed to discuss El Arish with Foreign Secretary Lansdowne.
Leopold Greenberg, Herzl's main negotiator, obtained the Foreign Office letter offering a colony with autonomy.
1903, Sixth Congress: 295-178 to send a commission to East Africa; Britain withdrew the offer in 1905.
19 June 1917: Balfour asked Rothschild and Weizmann for a draft; Weizmann had met him on 22 March.
Prime Minister from December 1916; the War Cabinet approved the declaration on 31 Oct 1917.
31 Oct 1917: the War Cabinet decision.
Lord Milner, War Cabinet minister without portfolio.
His late-August 1917 draft changed the scope to "in Palestine"; co-author of the 4 Oct Milner-Amery draft.
Leo Amery co-drafted the safeguard clauses with Milner (Oct 1917).
Claimed co-authorship of the final draft with Amery.
26 Oct 1917: Curzon's memorandum questioned what "National Home" would mean.
Under-Secretary Robert Cecil backed the policy by June 1917; 2 Dec 1917: "Judea [is] for the Jews."
Ronald Graham of the Foreign Office recorded on 13 June 1917 that the PM, Foreign Secretary and Cecil favoured the policy.
Sept 1917: Sykes reported to the War Cabinet after talks with Zionist leaders from Feb 1917.
Jan 1915: Samuel circulated "The Future of Palestine" to the Cabinet.
Prime Minister until Dec 1916; favoured reform of the Ottoman Empire over partition.
Foreign Secretary under Asquith.
23 Aug 1917: called Zionism "a mischievous political creed" and the declaration antisemitic.
Montagu's opposition modified the declaration's terms.
Cousins on opposite sides: Samuel the moderate Zionist, Montagu the opponent.
Edwin was a son of the 1st Baron Swaythling; Louis was the 2nd Baron.
6 May 1917: Benedict XV received Sokolow; per Sokolow's notes he expressed general sympathy, stressing the holy places.

19-26 April 1920: Japanese ambassador at San Remo.
Italian Prime Minister Nitti presided.
President of the French Council of Ministers (1920).
Prime Minister of Italy (1920).
Japan's ambassador.
25 April 1920: Britain named Mandatory for Palestine, to implement the Balfour Declaration while protecting non-Jewish communities' civil and religious rights.
High Commissioner for Palestine, 1 July 1920 - 30 June 1925.
High Commissioner for Palestine, 25 Aug 1925 - 31 July 1928.
High Commissioner for Palestine, (acting) 31 July - 6 Dec 1928.

19 May 1896: Herzl proposed extraterritorial status for the holy places to the nuncio in Vienna.
22 Jan 1904: the Secretary of State told Herzl the holy places could not be separated from the Holy Land.
25 Jan 1904: "We cannot prevent the Jews from going to Jerusalem but we could never sanction it."
Cardinal Secretary of State.
Apr-May 1917: Gasparri sought a "reserved zone" (Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Nazareth, Tiberias, Jericho).
1917: Sokolow met Msgr. Eugenio Pacelli, the future Pius XII.
Cardinal Secretary of State.
15 May 1922: note to the League opposing a "privileged and preponderant position" for Jews; 18 Dec 1917 he had opposed a Jewish state.
Mar 1943: the Holy See "has never approved" making Palestine a Jewish home.
May 1943: Cardinal Maglione suggested other territories for a Jewish homeland.
10 Apr 1945: Pius XII received Shertok but gave no support.
1948-49: three encyclicals calling for an internationally guaranteed Jerusalem, a campaign run with France.
1947: the Holy See avoided interfering, likely to protect the corpus separatum for Jerusalem.
5 Jan 1964: the first papal visit to Israel (no diplomatic relations until 1993-94).
